title: One Row of the Binomial Triangle
statement:
Build a triangle of numbers row by row. Row 0 is [1]. Each later row starts and ends with 1, and every inner number is the sum of the two numbers just above it in the previous row.

Given row, return that row of the triangle (rows are numbered from 0). Try to use only O(row) extra memory.

examples.why: Row 3 is [1, 3, 3, 1]; the inner values of row 4 are 1+3, 3+3 and 3+1.
Rows are numbered from 0, so row 0 is the single 1 at the top.

hints: You only ever need the row right above the one you are building.
You can even reuse one array: append a 1, then update the inner values. In which direction must you walk so you do not overwrite a value you still need?
Walk from right to left: row[j] += row[j − 1]. The left neighbour is still the old value when you read it.

explain.intuition:
Each row depends only on the row above, so keep one array and grow it in place. Append a 1 to the end, then turn the old row into the new one with row[j] = row[j] + row[j − 1] for the inner positions.

The direction matters. If you go left to right, row[j − 1] has already been updated to its new value by the time you read it. Going right to left reads row[j − 1] before it changes. This is the same trick as the 1-D knapsack: iterate so that you read old values before you overwrite them.
steps: Then for j from length − 2 down to 1, set row[j] += row[j − 1].
pitfalls: Updating left to right in the same array, which adds already-updated values.
Off by one on the row number: row 0 has one element, row k has k + 1.
Using the factorial formula directly. 33! overflows; the multiplicative formula or the additive build stays small.

solutions.title: Build every row
solutions.idea: Generate rows one after another from the previous row.

solutions.title: One array, right to left
solutions.idea: Append a 1, then add each left neighbour walking right to left so old values are read before they change.

solutions.title: Multiplicative formula
solutions.idea: Entry k is C(row, k), and C(row, k) = C(row, k − 1) · (row − k + 1) / k. The division is always exact.

followups: Why is the division in the multiplicative formula always exact? Where would it stop being safe with 64-bit floats?
Return only the k-th entry of a row with index up to 10⁹, modulo a prime.
